Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette: Sara, a 51-year-old married dentist of South Eastern Asian descent, has been grappling with intrusive memories and heightened anxiety since experiencing a traumatic stalking incident three months ago. The stalker’s persistent presence outside her home and office, coupled with the unsettling phone calls and texts, left Sara feeling perpetually on edge. Although the police were involved and eventually apprehended the individual, Sara remains deeply affected by the experience. One of the most potent triggers for Sara is certain songs that remind her of the period during which she was being stalked. For instance, one particular song that played frequently on the radio during that time now provokes a flood of memories and intense anxiety. Whenever she hears this song, whether in a commercial or while driving with the radio on, she immediately feels a surge of fear and panic. This reaction is not limited to music; exposure to media content related to stalking cases further exacerbates her sense of vulnerability. Sara’s husband has noticed that she becomes visibly distressed when these songs come on, and she often turns off the radio or changes channels abruptly. This avoidance behavior extends into her professional life as well. As a dentist, Sara finds herself particularly triggered during work hours if there are any mentions of safety protocols over the intercom or if there is an unexpected visit from police personnel who occasionally drop by to check on the security measures at the dental office. The presence of authority figures like police officers now triggers a heightened state of vigilance and anxiety for Sara. Their appearance, even in a professional capacity, brings back memories of the traumatic stalking experience and reinforces her belief that she cannot trust anyone’s assurances of safety. Even when colleagues or friends assure her that everything is under control, she finds it impossible to believe them. Her sense of unease is further amplified by her constant need for physical security. Sara always chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected she feels. In social gatherings or at work, she insists on sitting in a spot where she can see the door and any potential exits clearly. This behavior has become so ingrained that even casual settings like coffee shops or restaurants are now difficult for her to navigate comfortably. Her back must always be against a wall where she can maintain visual control over her surroundings. This constant need for safety and the overwhelming sense of threat have significantly impacted Sara’s daily life. She has become increasingly isolated, avoiding situations that might trigger her anxiety. This isolation has affected both her professional duties and personal relationships. She has canceled several social engagements and finds herself withdrawing from friends and family to minimize exposure to potential triggers. Despite the efforts to avoid these triggering scenarios, Sara remains haunted by the memories of her stalking experience. The pervasive sense of threat persists even in environments that others might perceive as safe. What frightens her most is the feeling that she will never be able to fully trust anyone’s assurances or feel genuinely secure again. It was a particularly distressing encounter at work, where a routine police visit led to an acute panic attack, that finally prompted Sara to seek help. She recognizes that this cycle of fear and avoidance has become debilitating and seeks therapy to regain control over her life. Her primary hope is to find ways to feel safe again and reconnect with the world without the constant burden of threat looming over her every action and decision.
